title: Ethereum Crypto Stack — Keccak-256, secp256k1, EIP-55, EIP-191

questions.question: Which statement best matches your current comfort level with Ethereum cryptography?
options: I can explain Keccak vs SHA3 and how Ethereum addresses are derived.
I can use web3 libraries, but I’m fuzzy on the exact byte-level steps.
I know Ethereum uses signatures and hashes, but not the details.
I’m new to both blockchains and cryptography.
questions.explanation: This is a pacing question. Any answer is fine; it helps choose how much detail to emphasize.

questions.question: In Python, which built-in hash most closely matches Ethereum’s keccak256?
options: hashlib.sha256
hashlib.sha3_256
There is no built-in Keccak-256 in hashlib
hashlib.md5
questions.explanation: Python’s stdlib includes SHA-3 (FIPS 202), but not Ethereum’s Keccak-256 variant.

questions.question: Why do Keccak-256 and SHA3-256 produce different digests for the same input?
options: They use different internal state sizes (1600 vs 1024 bits).
They use different padding/domain separation, even though both use Keccak-f[1600].
Keccak-256 is keyed and SHA3-256 is unkeyed.
SHA3-256 truncates the output but Keccak-256 does not.
questions.explanation: Ethereum uses Keccak-256 with a different suffix/padding than the standardized SHA3-256.

questions.question: How is an Ethereum EOA address derived from an uncompressed public key?
options: address = sha256(0x04 || X || Y)[12:]
address = keccak256(0x04 || X || Y)[12:]
address = keccak256(X || Y)[12:]
address = ripemd160(keccak256(X || Y))
questions.explanation: Ethereum drops the 0x04 prefix and hashes the 64 bytes X||Y, then keeps the last 20 bytes.

questions.question: EIP-55 checksums are encoded by:
options: Appending 4 checksum bytes to the address.
Base58Check encoding the address bytes.
Uppercasing hex letters based on the Keccak-256 hash of the lowercase hex address string.
Signing the address with ECDSA and embedding the signature.
questions.explanation: EIP-55 uses capitalization as a checksum derived from keccak256(lowercase_hex_address).

questions.question: What does EIP-191 (personal_sign) hash before signing?
options: keccak256(message)
keccak256("\x19Ethereum Signed Message:\n" + len(message) + message)
sha3_256("\x19Ethereum Signed Message:\n" + len(message) + message)
sha256(message)
questions.explanation: personal_sign prefixes the message with a length-bearing string and hashes with Keccak-256.

questions.question: Why do many Ethereum implementations enforce a 'low-s' rule for ECDSA signatures? (Attack-themed)
options: It prevents signature malleability where (r, s) and (r, n − s) both verify.
It makes signatures smaller in DER encoding.
It allows recovering the public key without extra data.
It converts ECDSA into a deterministic signature scheme.
questions.explanation: Because both s and (n−s) verify, enforcing low-s makes the signature canonical and removes a malleability vector.

questions.question: Which mismatch is most likely to cause a valid-looking signature to fail verification in an Ethereum integration?
options: Using UTF-16 instead of UTF-8 for the signed message bytes.
Verifying on the wrong message hash (e.g., raw bytes vs EIP-191 prefixed hash).
Using big-endian integer encoding for r and s.
Using a 32-byte hash instead of a 64-byte hash.
questions.explanation: Most real-world failures come from signing/verification hashing different byte sequences (prefixing and encoding).
